prompt: Why must `requests` and `limits` for `nvidia.com/gpu` be equal integers, when CPU happily allows a lower request than limit?
answer_markdown: CPU is a compressible resource: the kernel can hand a container smaller time slices, so a request of 500m with a limit of 2 means "you are guaranteed a little and may burst", and the container keeps running either way. A GPU is not compressible — the device plugin allocates a whole physical device to exactly one container, and there is no mechanism to give it a fraction of a card. Because there is no throttling behaviour to fall back on, the distinction between a guaranteed floor and a burst ceiling is meaningless, so Kubernetes requires the two values to match and rejects a Pod where they do not. The practical consequence is that GPUs cannot be overcommitted at all: the sum of GPU requests on a node can never exceed the number of devices it physically has, whereas you can safely overcommit CPU on the bet that not every container peaks at once.

prompt: Your GPU pod has been `Pending` for twenty minutes. Walk through how you diagnose it.
answer_markdown: Start with `kubectl describe pod` and read the scheduler's events, then check three things in order. First, does any node actually advertise the resource — `kubectl get nodes -o json` and look for `nvidia.com/gpu` in `status.allocatable`. If the key is absent everywhere, the problem is the driver or the device plugin DaemonSet, not your Pod, because Kubernetes has no built-in notion of a GPU and only learns about devices when the plugin registers them. Second, if nodes do advertise GPUs, check whether your Pod tolerates the GPU node's taint; the event will say `node(s) had untolerated taint`, which is one of the clearer messages you will get. Third, if a node has free devices and the Pod still will not schedule, check whether your `nodeSelector` is too narrow or whether the Pod's CPU and memory requests do not fit alongside existing Pods. A common red herring is `nvidia-smi` showing 0% utilisation: Kubernetes schedules on allocation, not utilisation, so a device held by a stuck Pod looks completely idle while being unavailable.

prompt: Why are GPU nodes almost always tainted, and what happens if you forget?
answer_markdown: A taint marks a node as repelling Pods unless they carry a matching toleration, and the point on a GPU node is to keep out everything that does not need the hardware. Without it, any ordinary CPU-only workload can be scheduled onto a GPU node — it never requests `nvidia.com/gpu`, so nothing about the GPU accounting stops it. Those Pods then consume the node's CPU, memory and local disk, which are exactly the host resources the GPU workload also needs to feed the device and to load weights. The result is that you pay a large hourly premium for accelerated hardware and it sits partly blocked by workloads that would run fine on a commodity node, and your actual GPU Pod may fail to schedule for want of CPU rather than for want of a device. The convention is a taint such as `nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule` plus a node label and matching `nodeSelector`, so GPU Pods land on the right card type and nothing else lands there at all.

prompt: You need to let three teams share a small pool of GPUs. Compare time-slicing and MIG, and say which you would choose for a production multi-tenant service.
answer_markdown: Time-slicing makes the device plugin advertise one physical GPU as several replicas, and the CUDA driver context-switches between the processes using them. It buys concurrency and nothing else: the replicas share a single pool of VRAM with no isolation, so one Pod loading a large model can push a neighbour into an out-of-memory crash, and latency becomes unpredictable because each process is competing for the whole device. MIG partitions supported data-centre cards into hardware-isolated instances with their own memory and compute paths, advertised as distinct resources like `nvidia.com/mig-1g.5gb`, so a misbehaving tenant genuinely cannot starve or crash another. For a production multi-tenant service I would choose MIG, accepting its constraints — fixed partition profiles and support only on certain cards — because the failure mode of time-slicing is a tenant taking down another tenant, which is not acceptable in production. Time-slicing is the right tool for development, notebooks and CI, where a crash is an inconvenience rather than an incident.

prompt: How does Kubernetes learn that a node has GPUs at all, and why does a driver problem surface as a confusing scheduling message?
answer_markdown: Kubernetes has no built-in concept of a GPU; accelerators are exposed through the device plugin framework. A vendor plugin runs as a DaemonSet on each GPU node, discovers the physical devices, and registers them with the kubelet, which then advertises them to the API server as an extended resource — an arbitrary named quantity the scheduler can count, such as `nvidia.com/gpu: 4`. The confusion when something breaks comes from how absence is represented: if the driver or plugin is unhealthy the node does not advertise `nvidia.com/gpu: 0`, the key is missing from `allocatable` entirely. From the scheduler's point of view you have asked for a resource that no node in the cluster offers, so it reports something like `0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu`. That message reads like a capacity problem and never mentions a driver, which is why engineers waste time hunting for free GPUs when the real fix is on the plugin's Pods and logs.

prompt: A colleague argues you should use time-slicing in production so more Pods fit per GPU and utilisation goes up. What is wrong with the reasoning, even though the utilisation goal is correct?
answer_markdown: The goal is right — a GPU costs the same idle as saturated, so utilisation is the cost lever — but time-slicing raises the Pod count without raising useful throughput, and it removes the isolation that makes the deployment safe. Time-sliced replicas share one pool of VRAM, so total memory does not grow: two Pods each expecting to load a model that nearly fills the card will simply make one of them fail, and which one fails is a race. Even when both fit, they contend for the whole device, so per-request latency becomes unpredictable in a way you cannot promise an SLO against. The better route to the same goal is raising utilisation *within* one server process — larger effective batch sizes via continuous batching, or serving multiple LoRA adapters over a shared base model — because that increases work done per device without splitting the device between processes that cannot see each other. If you genuinely need multiple isolated tenants on one card, MIG is the mechanism that provides it in hardware.
